agent-agent-harness.s: The definition that replaced the plain ReAct loop

k.d: The first idea of an agent: the model reasons, calls a tool, reads the result, and repeats until the task is done. Fine for short tasks; long tasks drift because the context fills with noise.
Everything you put around the model: instructions, skills, tools, memory, a filesystem, sub-agents and approvals. Its job is to get the model the right context at the right time.
Models are only as good as the context they get. A harness built for your domain (your skills, your tools, your checks) beats a bigger model with a generic prompt.

agent-agent-harness.t: Three layers of a production agent

k.d: What you bring: the expertise, written as instructions, skills and evals. This is where most of the value is and where teams should spend their time.
Where that expertise runs: the agent loop plus planning, files, sub-agents, memory and steering.
What makes it safe for many users: auth, multi-tenancy, durable execution, task queue, streaming, sandboxes, gateway, tracing and evals.
Models are good at reading and writing files, so the agent gets its own workspace for notes, plans and large tool outputs instead of keeping everything in the prompt.
When the agent writes code, it runs in an isolated sandbox with no secrets and limited network, so a mistake or an injection can't reach real systems.

Three levels: at start the agent sees only each skill's name and description; it reads the full SKILL.md when a task needs it; extra files load only when that body points to them. Deep Agents: name 1-64 lowercase characters, description up to 1,024; keep the body under ~500 lines.
The agent manages its own memory: what it learns for everyone (procedures) and what it knows about one user (preferences).
Deep Agents summarises when the conversation reaches 85% of the model's input limit, keeps the most recent 10% word for word, and writes the full history to the filesystem so nothing is lost.
In Deep Agents a tool result over 20,000 tokens is written to the backend and replaced by its file path plus a 10-line preview. The agent reads the parts it needs later.
The agent writes a plan (a todo list) and breaks the work into steps it can track and update.

The main agent hands work to a sub-agent through a task tool. The sub-agent works in its own context window (isolated by default) and the parent gets only the final result, not the dozens of tool calls. Anthropic suggests the summary back is often 1,000-2,000 tokens.
Mark risky tools (interrupt_on). The run pauses and a person approves, edits or rejects the call (or responds, for ask-the-user tools). This needs a checkpointer.

k.t: Why it can wait for days
k.d: interrupt() saves the state and waits indefinitely; resuming with the person's decision on the same thread re-runs that step from its start. So keep side effects before an interrupt idempotent.

agent-agent-harness.s: How one agent is laid out as files

k.d: The agent loop itself.
The core behaviour: who the agent is and how it works.
Playbooks for specific jobs, loaded on demand.
Connections to systems, often MCP servers.
Who can call the agent and which credentials each tool uses.
What the agent remembers, for whom, and where it is stored.
Saves the thread's state after steps (Postgres in production). Pick durability: sync (save before the next step), async (save while the next step runs) or exit (save only at the end).
LangGraph retry defaults: 3 attempts, 0.5 s first wait, doubling, capped at 128 s, with jitter.
On deploy, workers stop at a step boundary, save a checkpoint and the run resumes on another worker.
Every model call has a token budget. Long agent runs add tool results and turns until the budget is nearly gone.
Even before the limit, very long contexts make the model worse at finding what matters. Less, better context wins.
Move large tool outputs to files and keep a pointer.
Summarise older turns into a short state of play: decisions, open tasks, key facts.
Load skills, documents and memories just in time, not all up front.
Give noisy sub-tasks to sub-agents with their own window; take back a summary.
The goal, decisions made, open todos, file paths and IDs, errors still unresolved, and the most recent turns word for word.
Old raw tool output already saved to disk, repeated attempts, and chit-chat.
Keep the full history on disk so the agent can look something up again.
Trigger below the limit so there is room to write the summary. Deep Agents uses 85% of the input limit and keeps the newest 10%; it also summarises and retries if a call overflows.
Treat context as a finite attention budget: just-in-time loading, compaction into a fresh window, clearing old tool results, structured notes outside the window, and sub-agents.
Summarisation at 85%, 20,000-token tool results offloaded with a preview, skills by progressive disclosure, and an optional compact_conversation tool the agent can call itself.
The agent writes its todo list and working notes to files it can re-read later.
Big outputs are saved as files so the prompt stays small.
Long-term memory files (for example an AGENTS.md-style file) the agent reads at the start and updates over time.
Files live in the thread's checkpointed state: per conversation.
Files in a LangGraph store, across conversations; a namespace per user or per agent.
Files under a root folder; virtual mode keeps paths inside it.
Adds an execute tool that runs commands in isolation (e.g. LangSmith, Daytona).
Route by path prefix: /memories/ to the store, the rest to state.

agent-agent-filesystem.d: List, read, write and edit files, plus glob and grep to search them, the same moves a developer makes.

agent-context-hub.d: A shared, versioned home for an agent's instructions and skills, so business experts and engineers edit the same context.

k.d: The people who know the domain write and review the skills; engineers don't have to be the bottleneck.
Every change is a version you can diff, test and roll back.
A good skill made for one agent can be promoted to the whole workspace.

agent-context-hub.d: Run evals on every new version before it reaches users, and keep who changed what in the history.

agent-run-config.d: Settings passed with each run (model, tools, prompt variant, user or team) so one agent definition behaves differently depending on where it was called.

k.d: Build the agent on the fly per run: a different tool set for a channel, a cheaper model for a simple request.
Pass the caller's identity and channel so tools and memory use the right scope.
Private DMs and shared channels. The channel type changes which credentials and memories are safe to use.
Issues, pull requests and comments can start runs (shown in the talk; Managed Deep Agents docs list Slack and HTTP today).
A plain API spec so you can plug in any custom surface.
Timed runs from schedule files (five-field cron, UTC unless set), and schedules the agent creates itself through a custom tool.
Normalise every channel into the same run request: who, where, what.
Stream progress back to the same place; send private prompts (like sign-in links) only to the person.

agent-agent-auth-handler.d: A central auth handler checks each request from any channel and sets the principal: a user, or the agent itself.
The principal travels with the run so every tool, memory and credential lookup knows who it is acting for.

k.d: Prove who is calling (SSO, signed webhooks, API keys).
Decide which threads, agents and data that caller may touch; filter on the server, every time.

agent-agent-auth-handler.d: An authenticate handler returns the caller's identity; authorization handlers (threads, assistants, store) tag owners on create and filter reads, returning 403 to deny. Identity keys a client tries to send are stripped.

k.d: The agent acts as you, with your own OAuth token: your CRM, your inbox. It can only see what you can see.
The agent acts as itself with a service account. Use it in shared places so nobody's private access leaks.

agent-credential-broker.d: The broker picks the token from the principal and the channel: DM -> user token, shared channel -> agent token. Tokens never enter the prompt.

In Managed Deep Agents a missing user grant raises one interrupt (credential_authorization_required) with a connect link; when the user finishes OAuth the run resumes. Slack and Studio show this for you.

k.d: An agent with broad access doing something for a user who shouldn't have it. Fix: user-scoped tokens and least privilege.
Never put secrets in prompts, logs or memory; inject them at the tool boundary.

agent-credential-broker.t: How tools ask for a token
agent-credential-broker.d: A tool asks for a connection by name and owner type (user or agent) and never passes a user ID; the runtime works out who the caller is. Types: plain secret, OAuth, MCP OAuth.

llmops-agent-eval-harness.d: An agent takes many steps and changes things. You judge the end state and the path, not one reply.

k.d: An instruction like a real user's request.
A container or sandbox with the files, tools and services the agent needs.
Code that checks the result: tests pass, the file is right, the ticket was updated.
The steps, tool calls, tokens and time, for cost and behaviour checks.

llmops-agent-eval-harness.d: Collect real tasks, build evals, change skills or prompts, hill-climb the score, ship, and feed production traces back into the dataset.

k.d: A framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench for evaluating and optimising agents; the official harness for Terminal-Bench 2.0. It runs agents like Claude Code, OpenHands or Codex CLI.
instruction.md, task.toml, an environment folder (Dockerfile or compose), a reference solution and tests. The verifier writes a score to reward.txt.
A set of trials; one trial is one agent attempt at one task, run in Docker locally or cloud sandboxes.

agent-agent-task-queue.d: Agent runs take minutes. Put runs on a queue so web requests return fast, bursts wait, and workers scale on their own.
In LangSmith Agent Server, concurrent runs = queue workers x jobs per worker (default 10). Postgres holds runs, threads, checkpoints and memory; Redis streams output from workers to API servers.

agent-agent-task-queue.s: A second message arrives while a run is going

k.d: Refuse the new run.
Run it after the current one.
Stop the current run, keep its progress, add the new input.
Stop, undo the current run's progress and start fresh.

agent-agent-task-queue.d: Create a run, get 'pending' back, then join, poll or stream it.

_what.agent-agent-harness: Everything you put around a model so it can do long, real tasks: instructions, skills, tools, a filesystem, sub-agents, memory and human steering. Agent = model + harness.
_what.agent-context-compaction: Keeps a long agent run inside its context budget by offloading, summarising, selecting and isolating context.
_what.agent-agent-filesystem: A workspace the agent reads and writes: plans, notes, memories and big tool outputs live in files instead of the prompt.
_what.agent-context-hub: A versioned, shared home for an agent's instructions and skills, edited by experts and promoted through staging to production.
_what.agent-run-config: Settings sent with each run (model, tools, variant) so one agent behaves right for each caller and channel.
_what.agent-agent-channels: The places an agent is called from - chat, webhooks, schedules - normalised into one run request.
_what.agent-agent-auth-handler: Decides who is calling the agent and carries that principal through the run so every tool and memory uses the right scope.
_what.agent-credential-broker: Hands each tool call the right token: the user's own (act as me) or the agent's service account (act as the agent).
_what.llmops-agent-eval-harness: Scores agents on real tasks in a sandboxed environment with a verifier, not on single answers.
_what.agent-agent-task-queue: Holds agent runs until a worker is free, so long runs scale, retry and stay fair.

fe-csr-spa-client-render.s: Shell first, everything else in the browser

k.d: The minimal HTML plus script tags that every route shares. Because it is identical for all URLs, it can be cached forever on a CDN.
HTML, then JS, then data, then render. Each step waits for the previous one, so the order of requests matters more than any single one.
Kick off data requests in the router loader or from a server-provided promise, not inside a component after it mounts.
Use modulepreload or prefetch for the route chunk the user will probably open next.
The client built the DOM itself, so handlers are attached as it renders. That removes the double-work of server-rendered apps.
A cap on bytes shipped for the first route, enforced in CI. web.dev suggests keeping critical-path resources around 170 KB compressed for slow networks.
Dynamic import() creates a chunk per route or heavy component, so the landing screen does not pay for the settings page.
The most common cut line. The router lazy-loads the page module when the URL matches.
Charts, editors and maps load on demand, usually behind an interaction or visibility.
File names contain a content hash, so they can be cached as immutable. Only index.html is revalidated on every visit.
Bots that do not execute JavaScript see an empty shell. Use prerendering or SSR for public pages.
All rendering work runs on the user's device, so low-end phones feel the cost of every extra KB.
Open tabs may reference chunks that no longer exist after a release. Handle chunk-load failure by prompting a reload.

fe-ssg-static-pages.s: Static means decided before the request

k.d: Static rendering writes final HTML per URL at build time. Prerendering a client app captures initial HTML, but the page still needs its JS to become interactive.
A route like /blog/[slug] needs the full list of slugs at build time, supplied by a function such as generateStaticParams.
In a pure export, any param not listed returns 404. A runtime framework can generate it on first request instead.
HTML, CSS, JS and images in one folder, deployable to any static host or object store plus CDN.
Files are copied to many locations, so the byte path is short and no origin compute is involved.
Hashed JS and CSS can be immutable for a year; HTML gets a short or revalidated lifetime so new deploys appear.
After load, JavaScript calls an API for per-user or live data and fills reserved space to avoid layout shift.
Astro hydrates only components marked with client directives, and server islands render personalised parts on demand while the rest stays static.
Hydrate when the component scrolls into view - good for below-the-fold widgets.
Page renders at once with a fallback; the island's HTML arrives from a separate request and swaps in.
CMS webhooks and CI pipelines rebuild when content changes. For large sites, move hot routes to ISR.
Inside the revalidate window the cached page is served and nothing else happens.
Past the window the page is still served, but the request triggers a background render. This is stale-while-revalidate.
A successful render swaps the entry. A failed render leaves the old page in place and is retried later.

fe-isr-revalidate.s: Choose by how precise you need to be

k.d: export const revalidate = 3600 on a route. Simple, predictable load, content can lag by the window.
Called from a Server Action, route handler or webhook.
Invalidates a route; the next request regenerates it. Good for 'this page changed'.
Invalidates every cached fetch or function tagged with a label, across many pages. Good for 'this article changed'.
The x-nextjs-cache header reports HIT, STALE, MISS or REVALIDATED, which is the first thing to check when debugging.
Use a custom cache handler so multiple instances share entries and invalidations.
During rolling deploys a client from build A may hit a server on build B. A deployment id lets the client fall back to a hard navigation.

fe-streaming-ssr-suspense.s: Shell first, then boundary by boundary

k.d: Everything that renders before any async work resolves: layouts, navigation and Suspense fallbacks.
A marker around a component that may wait. While it waits React shows the fallback; when ready it streams the finished HTML and swaps it in.
Next.js file convention that wraps a page in a boundary automatically - good when nothing renders without the data.
Sibling boundaries stream independently; nested ones create progressive detail, such as product first then reviews.
The HTTP mechanism that lets the server send the body in pieces without knowing its total length.

fe-streaming-ssr-suspense.s: What improves and what can regress

k.d: Drop to the time needed to render the shell instead of the slowest query.
Only improves if the LCP element is in the shell. Inside a boundary it waits for the swap.
Use fallbacks with matching dimensions to avoid shift on swap.
Selective hydration splits work into small tasks, keeping the main thread responsive.
Reverse proxies, CDNs, compression and serverless platforms may hold chunks. Verify in the Network tab or by reading the response as a stream.
Fixed after the first chunk. Do hard checks first, use error boundaries for failures mid-stream.
HTML-limited crawlers get metadata in the initial HTML; the server waits for it before sending the page.

fe-react-server-components.s: Where code runs decides what it can do

k.d: Runs once on the server (build time or per request). Can be async, read data and use secrets. Cannot use state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs.
await data in the component body; React suspends until it resolves, which works naturally with streaming.
Start a fetch on the server without awaiting, pass the promise to a Client Component and read it with use() inside Suspense.
Marked with 'use client'. Has state, effects and handlers. It is also prerendered to HTML on the server, then hydrated.
Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable. Functions can only cross as Server Functions.
A Client Component such as Modal receives server-rendered children, so the content stays on the server.
Wrap children in a small Client Component provider placed deep in the tree.
Wrap them in your own 'use client' file so they can be used from Server Components.
Packages that cause a build error if a module is imported on the wrong side.
Functions with 'use server' called from forms or event handlers. Forms still work before hydration (progressive enhancement).
Check authentication and authorisation and validate input in every action.
CVE-2025-55182 (CVSS 10.0) allowed unauthenticated RCE in affected React 19 versions; upgrade to patched releases of React and your framework.
Event listeners, the component tree and application state, usually by re-downloading and re-running component code.
The client must render the same output as the server.
Dates, typeof window checks, matchMedia, and different data on server and client.
suppressHydrationWarning for a single unavoidable difference; a two-pass render with useEffect for client-only content; fix data sources.
With Suspense, React hydrates boundaries independently and prioritises the one the user touches.
Interactive components hydrated separately, possibly with different UI frameworks on one page.
load (high priority), idle (medium), visible (low, IntersectionObserver), media (breakpoint), only (skip SSR).
server:defer renders dynamic parts on demand with a fallback, keeping the page shell cacheable.
State, listeners and closures are written into HTML so the browser can continue where the server stopped.
One tiny listener reads attributes like on:click pointing to chunk#symbol and downloads it on demand.
Code must be serialisable: class instances and streams stay client-only. It requires a different programming style.

fe-app-shell-router.s: Change the view, not the page

k.d: pushState adds an entry, replaceState overwrites the current one, and popstate fires on Back and Forward.
Anchor clicks are prevented and handed to the router, keeping real hrefs for accessibility, open in new tab and crawlers.
Every URL must work on first load, so the server returns the app or prerendered HTML for any route.
Children inherit the parent's path and render into its Outlet.
Layout routes share chrome without adding a URL segment; index routes are the default child at the parent's URL.
Parts like :teamId become params passed to loaders and components.
Each route is a lazy chunk. Combine with prefetching for the likely next page.
Fetch at the router level so code and data load together, not one after the other.
Keep the old view during a transition, show a delayed indicator, and use skeletons for slow content.
Owns the shell: layout, routing, authentication, error handling and loading of remotes.
A separately built and deployed app that exposes modules, such as a page or widget, through a remote entry file.
A registry of libraries (like React) that builds provide and consume instead of bundling private copies.
exposes lists modules a build offers (keys start with ./). remotes maps a name to name@url.
When the URL is only known at runtime, load the entry script yourself, init the share scope, then call get().
singleton (one version), requiredVersion (range), eager (bundle into entry, can bloat), shareScope (name).
A consumer gets the highest version satisfying its range; below the range logs a warning.
Remote modules always need a chunk load, so the host imports them lazily.
Prefer props, custom events and the URL. Keep coupling low and test the contract.
BEM naming, CSS modules, CSS-in-JS or Shadow DOM so teams cannot override each other.
Error boundary and fallback around each remote; canary releases; monitoring per slice.
Automation for pipelines, shared linting and a design system to prevent drift.
JSON where each token has a $value and optional $type (colour, dimension, fontFamily, shadow, typography and more). Groups organise tokens; aliases like {group.token} reference another token.
Raw values, such as blue-500.
Meaningful roles, such as color-action, that alias primitives.
Optional overrides scoped to one component.
A build tool transforms the JSON into CSS variables, and into iOS or Android formats when needed.
The Design Tokens Format Module 2025.10 is a Community Group draft, not yet a W3C Standard.
Small and composable: variants, sizes and slots rather than dozens of one-off props.
Keyboard support, visible focus, correct roles and contrast are the component's job, not each product's.
Custom properties are inherited and resolved at use. Redefine them under prefers-color-scheme or [data-theme] for dark mode; var() fallbacks cover undefined values.
A workshop for building components in isolation. Each story is one state; docs are generated, and stories double as test cases.
Interaction, accessibility, visual and snapshot tests run in CI against stories.
Semantic versioning, changelog, deprecations and codemods; 'use client' at entry points for Server Component compatibility.
Ownership, a contribution path, and adoption metrics so the system stays useful instead of becoming a bottleneck.

fe-global-store-zustand-redux.s: Put each piece of state in the right home

k.d: useState or useReducer inside one component. Start here; it is the simplest and cheapest.
Data only the app owns and many components share: theme, sidebar, wizard step, draft. This is what a global store is for.
Data that lives on the server and arrives asynchronously. It needs caching and refetching, so it belongs in a server-state cache, not the store.
Filters, tabs and page numbers that should survive refresh and be shareable as links.
Values, errors and touched flags of a form, usually handled by a form library.

fe-global-store-zustand-redux.s: How the library keeps things predictable

k.d: A hook-based store: create() takes state and actions, set() merges updates, and no provider is needed.
A function that picks a slice of state. The component re-renders only when that slice changes.
Add-ons wrapped around the store, such as persist (saves to storage) and devtools.
The official way to write Redux. A single store, plain-object actions and pure reducers, with less code.
Generates action creators and reducers from one definition; Immer lets you write update code that looks like mutation but stays immutable.
Sets up the store, thunk middleware, dev-mode mutation checks and Redux DevTools in one call.
Ready-made reducers and selectors for normalized collections (ids plus entities).
Built into React. Good for rarely-changing values; every consumer re-renders when the value changes, so it is weaker for fast-moving state.

fe-global-store-zustand-redux.s: Keep renders small and state safe

k.d: Select the smallest slice, derive values in selectors, and pass ids to children so each one selects its own data.
Save chosen fields to localStorage or similar. Use partialize to pick fields, version and migrate to survive shape changes, and skipHydration in server-rendered apps to avoid mismatches.
Log every action and replay state changes (time travel) to debug how the state got where it is.

fe-server-state-cache-tanstack-query.s: The life of a cache entry

k.d: Within staleTime the cached data is used as-is with no refetch.
After staleTime (default 0) data is shown instantly but refetched on triggers. This is stale-while-revalidate.
When no component uses a query it becomes inactive and is deleted after gcTime (default 5 minutes).
A new component mounting, window focus and network reconnect each refetch stale queries. refetchInterval adds polling.
A top-level array that is JSON-serializable and includes every variable the queryFn uses.
Object key order does not matter; array item order does. A property set to undefined matches a key without it.
Build keys in one helper (['todos','list',filters]) so a prefix invalidates a whole family and typos are impossible.

fe-server-state-cache-tanstack-query.s: What the library does for you

k.d: Many components using the same key share one request and one cache entry.
3 retries by default (0 on the server) with exponential backoff: 1 s doubling, capped at 30 s.
invalidateQueries marks matches stale (overriding staleTime) and refetches active ones. Prefix matching by default, exact: true to narrow, predicate for custom logic.
Unchanged parts of refetched JSON keep their object reference, so React skips needless re-renders.
Create the QueryClient per request so users never share a cache.
Prefetch on the server, serialise the cache with dehydrate, and restore it in HydrationBoundary on the client.
Avoids refetching immediately on the client what the server just fetched.
Treat the client store like a small database: a table per type, items keyed by id, relationships stored as ids.
Rebuilding the nested shape a component wants from the flat store when it reads.
Avoids duplication, simplifies updates, and limits re-renders to what really changed.
Apollo's default is __typename and id (or _id) joined by a colon. If none can be built, the object stays nested in its parent.
Nested objects are replaced by __ref pointers to the stored entry.
Same id means incoming fields overwrite and others are kept.
Relay's convention: a Node interface with a globally unique, opaque id and a node(id:) query to refetch any object.
Redux's explicit shape: items by id plus an array for order. Redux Toolkit's entity adapter uses ids and entities.
Good for one-direction relationships with no data of their own, like an author's bookIds.
For many-to-many or relationships that carry data (an author's role on a book).
Add something like bookIdsByAuthorId only if profiling shows a bottleneck, updated by the same actions.
Creates and deletes change list membership; update the list field explicitly or refetch.
evict removes an object; gc removes everything unreachable from the root. retain keeps chosen objects alive.
References left pointing at evicted objects; handle with read functions.

fe-graphql-client.s: Data needs live with the component

k.d: Each component declares a fragment (e.g. AuthorDetails_author). Parents spread child fragments, so needs nest up the tree into one query.
A component can read only its own fragment fields. In Apollo turn it on with dataMasking: true; Relay does it by design.
Removing a field from a child cannot silently break a parent that never declared it.
Apollo's @unmask directive lets existing code keep working while you adopt masking step by step.
A live view of the cache for one fragment. It never hits the network; the parent query fills the cache.

fe-graphql-client.s: Pick by app size and needs

k.d: Flexible, large ecosystem, normalized InMemoryCache, a link chain for auth and retry.
Compiler-driven and strict: static queries, fragment masking, normalized store, global object ids. Built for large apps.
Lightweight and extensible. Default document cache, with the normalized Graphcache as an add-on.

fe-graphql-client.s: Send an id, not the text

k.d: Hash first; on PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND resend with the text. Needs no server setup and shrinks repeat requests.
Operations are registered ahead of time and the router can reject anything else (safelisting).
Hashed queries can go over GET so a CDN caches them; mutations and full-length queries stay POST.
Read the normalized cache first, then the network on a miss or when stale.
Middleware pieces for auth headers, retries, errors and persisted-query hashing.
Apollo stores a guessed result as a separate layer and removes it when the real response arrives or fails.
React state holds each value; every keystroke re-renders. Simple to reason about, slower for big forms.
The DOM holds the value and you read it on submit or through refs. React Hook Form's default model.
Connects a native input by name and attaches rules. Errors appear in formState.errors.
A wrapper for controlled UI-kit components such as MUI or React-Select that do not expose a plain input ref.
onSubmit (default), onBlur, onChange, onTouched, all. The docs warn onChange can hurt performance.
After a failed submit, fields with errors re-validate; default onChange.
Initial values, plain or async. They are cached, so use reset() to change them.

fe-form-state-validation.s: One definition for rules and types

k.d: TypeScript-first schemas: parse or safeParse untrusted data and infer the static type from the schema.
Plugs a schema library into the form library; it returns values and errors, with error keys matching field names.
Reuse the same schema in the API or Server Action so rules never drift.
Map them back to fields (setError) or return them as state from a form action (useActionState).
Tie messages to inputs, announce them, and focus the first invalid field.
React form actions with Server Functions can submit before JavaScript loads (permalink option).
Disable the button while pending and use an idempotency key for the request.
Search text, filters, sort, page, selected tab or item - anything someone would share or return to.
Secrets, tokens, personal data, large objects and throwaway UI state. URLs land in logs, history and referrers.
Path identifies the resource (/products/42); query refines the view (?sort=price).
get returns the first value or null, getAll returns all, set replaces, append adds, toString serialises. Use append rather than building strings, since a plus sign reads as a space.
Serialising percent-encodes special characters and turns spaces into plus signs; parsing decodes them. Always pass unencoded values to the API.
pushState adds an entry (Back works); replaceState edits the current one. Neither fires popstate; Back and Forward do.
Next.js: useSearchParams (read-only client hook) and the page searchParams prop. Update by building a new string and calling router.push or a Link.
Parse to typed values with defaults and fallbacks. TanStack Router's validateSearch does this per route.
Keep top-level keys flat strings so other tools can read them; encode nested values as URL-safe JSON if needed.
Omit a param when it equals its default, so URLs stay short and canonical.
Pages read searchParams on the server so the first paint matches the URL; in Next.js a static page using useSearchParams needs a Suspense boundary.
Put the params in the data query key so each combination caches on its own.
Debounce text input and use replace so the Back button stays useful.
Render the expected result before the server confirms, because most requests succeed.
Mark guessed items (for example pending: true) so users and tests can tell them from confirmed data.
If the request fails, return to the last known good state and tell the user.
Replace the guess with the server's response, such as the real id, and invalidate to be sure.
Returns optimisticState and a setter. It equals the real value unless an Action is pending; when the Action ends React renders the real value, so a failure reverts automatically.
A reducer receives the latest real value on every re-run, so use it for relative changes and lists; an updater only sees the state from when the transition started.
Call the setter inside startTransition or an Action prop, never during render, and keep reducers pure.
Render the pending mutation's variables. No cache change, so nothing to roll back; use useMutationState to show them elsewhere.
Write the guess in onMutate so every component updates.
Cancel outgoing refetches, snapshot the previous data, write the optimistic value, return the snapshot.
Restore the snapshot from the returned context.
Invalidate the query to sync with the server whether it worked or not.
A guessed result stored as a separate layer; removed when the real response arrives or an error occurs. New objects use a temporary id.
Likes, toggles, reorders, comments: high success rate, easy to undo.
Payments, irreversible deletes, anything the server often rejects.
Pair with a mutation queue so optimistic changes survive reconnecting.

fe-api-client-retry-abort.s: Never let a request run forever or land late

k.d: An object with a signal you pass to fetch. Calling abort() cancels the request and rejects the promise with an AbortError.
Makes a signal that aborts itself after the time, with a TimeoutError. It counts active time, so it pauses while the page is in the back-forward cache.
Combines signals so the request stops when the user cancels or the timeout fires, whichever is first.
Keep the latest controller in a variable and abort it before starting a new request (typeahead, route changes). Ignore AbortError in the catch block.
Abort listeners keep a signal alive, so remove them when the work finishes.

fe-api-client-retry-abort.s: Recover from blips without causing outages

k.d: Network errors, 429, 502, 503 and 504 are transient. 400, 401, 403 and 404 will fail the same way, so fail fast. Refresh the token once on 401 instead of retrying blindly.
Wait longer after each failure (1 s, 2 s, 4 s ...) up to a cap, and add randomness so many clients do not retry in lockstep.
A response header with seconds or a date. When present on 429 or 503, use it instead of your own delay.
Limit total retries (a token bucket or a max attempt count) so a long outage does not turn into a retry flood.
An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. POST is not, so send an Idempotency-Key and let the server deduplicate.
Hooks that run on every request or response: add the auth header, refresh an expired token, map errors to a common shape, log timing.
If two components ask for the same URL at once, share one in-flight promise. Server-state libraries do this by query key.
fetch only rejects on network failure, not on HTTP 4xx or 5xx. Check response.ok and throw a typed error so callers can branch on status.

fe-websocket-client.s: A small state machine you own

k.d: CONNECTING, OPEN, CLOSING, CLOSED. Only send when OPEN; otherwise buffer.
open, message, error and close. The close event gives code, reason and wasClean, which decide whether to retry.
1000 is a normal close, 1001 going away, 1006 an abnormal drop with no Close frame, 1008 a policy violation. Retry on drops; do not loop on policy or auth failures.
Always use the encrypted form in production. Plain ws:// is blocked on https pages as mixed content.
The browser API has no ping method, so send a tiny app message every few seconds and expect a pong. Timeout means dead.
Protocol-level control frames with at most 125 bytes of payload. A peer must answer a Ping with a Pong, so server-side pings are free of client code.
Delay grows each attempt up to a cap, with randomness. Reset the delay after a stable connection.
Mobile and sleeping tabs lose sockets. Reconnect on visibilitychange or online events, and close cleanly on pagehide.

fe-websocket-client.s: Keep data correct and the UI responsive

k.d: Send {type, id, seq, payload} so the client can route, deduplicate and detect gaps.
Track the last seq; on reconnect send it so the server replays missed events, or refetch a snapshot if too old.
The classic API cannot slow the sender. Check bufferedAmount before sending, and batch or throttle incoming updates before rendering.
Set binaryType to arraybuffer to receive binary frames as ArrayBuffer instead of Blob.

fe-sse-client-eventsource.s: Plain UTF-8 text over one HTTP response

k.d: Content-Type: text/event-stream, plus Cache-Control: no-cache. The server keeps the response open.
event, data, id and retry. Consecutive data lines are joined with newlines. A blank line ends the event; a line starting with a colon is a comment.
Sets the last event id the browser will send back on reconnect.
Tells the browser how many milliseconds to wait before reconnecting.
An event: line gives the event a type. Listen with addEventListener(type); unnamed events go to onmessage.

fe-sse-client-eventsource.s: The built-in API and its limits

k.d: CONNECTING (0), OPEN (1), CLOSED (2). close() ends it for good.
The browser reconnects after a drop and sends Last-Event-ID. A non-200 status or wrong content type is fatal; 204 means stop.
GET only, no custom headers; withCredentials is the only option. For POST or a Bearer token, stream a fetch response instead.

fe-sse-client-eventsource.s: Make it survive the real network

k.d: About 6 per domain on HTTP/1.1 across tabs; around 100 streams on HTTP/2.
Disable response buffering and send a comment roughly every 15 s so idle streams are not dropped.
Send small delta events and append them to state. Handle error events and unknown event types gracefully, and let users stop generation by aborting the request.
Close the stream when the tab is hidden and reconnect with the last id when it returns, to save connections and battery.
Base it on how stale the data may be. Faster polling multiplies requests by every open tab and user.
Conditional requests: the server sends an ETag, the client replies with If-None-Match, and an unchanged resource returns 304 with no body.
End polling when the job is completed or failed, on unmount, or after a maximum duration. Show a timeout message instead of polling forever.

fe-polling-long-polling.s: Hold the request until there is news

k.d: The server defers its response until an event or timeout, replies, and the client sends a new request at once.
Full HTTP headers on every message, a held connection per client, and latency of up to a few network trips. RFC 6202 lists these.
Keep the hold time below proxy limits; RFC 6202 calls about 30 s safe. Return an empty 200 or 204 on timeout and re-ask.
Send Cache-Control: no-cache so a long poll is never served from a cache.
Lengthen the interval while nothing changes, and add random offsets so clients do not synchronise.
Pause when document.hidden is true and refetch on visibilitychange. Hidden-tab timers are throttled by browsers anyway.
TanStack Query has refetchInterval, plus refetch on window focus and reconnect, so you rarely write the loop yourself.
{id, type, payload, createdAt, attempts, status}. The id is generated on the client and is also the idempotency key.
pending, sending, synced, failed. Show pending items in the UI so users trust that nothing is lost.
Use IndexedDB so the queue survives reloads and is readable from a service worker. Ask for persistent storage so the browser does not evict it.
App start, the online event, a timer with backoff, and the service worker sync event where supported.
registration.sync.register(tag) asks the browser to fire a sync event in the service worker when the network is stable. Limited availability, so keep a fallback.
Process one item at a time per entity so an update never runs before its create.
The server stores processed keys and returns the earlier result for a repeat. A concurrent retry can get 409, a reused key with a different body 422, per the IETF draft.
Back off with jitter on transient errors. Move permanent errors to a failed list the user can act on.

fe-offline-queue-outbox.s: What happens when two edits meet

k.d: Last write wins is simplest but can lose data. Field-level merge keeps more. Asking the user is safest for important documents. CRDTs avoid conflicts but are heavier.
Apply the change locally at once with a pending marker, and reconcile when the server answers.
Workbox Background Sync Queue for plain requests; TanStack Query mutations with networkMode for app-level mutations; a sync engine when you need merging.
header, nav, main, footer give screen reader users a page map. One h1 and a logical heading order let them jump by heading.
A first-in-DOM link to main content lets keyboard users bypass repeated navigation (WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks).
Every control needs an accessible name (label, aria-label, text), a role and a state. Native inputs with a label element get all three.
Visible label tied with for/id, errors linked with aria-describedby, required state in text and not colour alone.
Prefer native; do not change native semantics; every interactive ARIA control must work by keyboard; do not hide focusable elements.
role says what it is, aria-expanded or aria-selected say its state, aria-labelledby and aria-describedby give its name and help text.
The WAI-ARIA APG documents keyboard and ARIA for tabs, menu, combobox, dialog, accordion. Copy the pattern, do not invent one.
role=status or aria-live=polite for advisory updates, role=alert for urgent ones. Insert the region empty first, then change its text.

fe-accessibility-a11y.s: Every action reachable without a mouse

k.d: Follow DOM order. tabindex=0 joins the sequence, -1 allows script focus only; avoid positive values.
A clear focus indicator (WCAG 2.4.7). WCAG 2.2 adds that focus must not be hidden by sticky headers or banners (2.4.11).
Roving tabindex moves real focus between items with arrow keys. aria-activedescendant keeps focus on a container such as a combobox input.
Move focus in on open, trap Tab, close on Escape, restore focus to the trigger. On client route changes move focus to the new page heading.

fe-accessibility-a11y.s: Contrast, zoom, and how to prove it

k.d: 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large text and UI component boundaries (1.4.11); 24 by 24 px targets (2.5.8); content reflows at 400 percent zoom or 320px width.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-color-scheme; avoid autoplay and content that flashes.
eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y in the editor, axe-core in unit and end-to-end tests, Lighthouse in CI. Automation finds only part of real issues.
Unplug the mouse and complete key flows; test with VoiceOver, NVDA or TalkBack; check at 200 percent zoom.
Key to message maps per locale (en.json, fr.json). Keys are stable ids or the source sentence; add a description for translators.
A tool scans code for message ids, writes the source catalog, and CI fails on missing or unused keys.
Named placeholders plus plural, select and selectordinal in one string, e.g. {n, plural, =0 {No photos} one {# photo} other {# photos}}.
zero, one, two, few, many, other. Each language uses a subset; other is always present. Never assume 'one means 1' in every language.
Intl.NumberFormat (currency, percent, units, compact) and Intl.DateTimeFormat (date styles, time zones). Pass explicit timeZone; store UTC.
Intl.RelativeTimeFormat gives '3 days ago'; Intl.ListFormat gives 'A, B, and C' in the right language.
Intl.Collator compares strings by locale rules (accents, case); Intl.Segmenter splits words or graphemes in languages with no spaces.
Intl.DisplayNames translates region, language and currency names so you need not ship your own lists.
Set lang and dir on the html element; dir=auto can help for user-generated text of unknown direction.
margin-inline-start, padding-inline, inset-inline-end, text-align: start. Flex and grid already follow direction.
Arrows, back/forward icons, progress bars and slide animations flip; logos, media controls and numerals usually do not.
Translations can be much longer or shorter than English. Avoid fixed widths and test with pseudo-localization.

fe-i18n-l10n.s: Getting the right language to the right user

k.d: URL segment first, then saved preference, then Accept-Language; offer a visible language switcher and a redirect only on first visit.
Separate URLs per locale with hreflang alternates, a localized title and description, and lang on html.
Lazy-load the locale catalog, split big namespaces by route, and make SSR and client use the same messages to avoid hydration mismatch.

fe-csp-xss-defence.s: How script gets onto your page

k.d: Stored (saved then served to everyone), reflected (echoed from the request), DOM-based (client code writes input into a sink).
innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write, insertAdjacentHTML, eval, setTimeout with a string, script src, and href with javascript: URLs.
Anything script can reach: DOM, non-HttpOnly cookies, localStorage, and authenticated API calls made as the user.
HTML text, attributes, JavaScript, URLs and CSS each need different encoding; one escape function does not fit all.

fe-csp-xss-defence.s: Stop the bug at the source

k.d: Use textContent and framework templating. Treat dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, bypassSecurityTrust and unsafeHTML as red flags in review.
DOMPurify with an allow-list; keep config strict; never edit the string after sanitising; keep the library patched.
Allow only http, https (and mailto where needed) in user-supplied links; reject javascript: and data: schemes.
Render Markdown to HTML then sanitise the output, or use a renderer that emits React elements instead of raw HTML strings.
trustedTypes.createPolicy('app', { createHTML: s => DOMPurify.sanitize(s) }) is the only place that turns strings into TrustedHTML.
require-trusted-types-for 'script' makes plain strings throw; trusted-types lists allowed policy names.
A policy named default catches stray strings; use it to find old code during migration, not as the final design.
Baseline 2026 newly available; a tiny fallback keeps code running where the API is missing.

fe-csp-xss-defence.s: Browser-enforced allow-list of what may run

k.d: script-src 'nonce-RANDOM' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'. Nonce must be fresh and unguessable on every response.
A SHA-256 or similar hash of each inline script, plus integrity on external ones; good for static pages.
Report-only header first, Reporting-Endpoints plus report-to for collecting violations, then enforce. Report-only cannot be set via meta.
Subresource Integrity for CDN files, frame-ancestors against clickjacking, sandbox on iframes for untrusted content.
Opaque id in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie; the server holds the data and can revoke instantly.
__Host- prefix (Secure, Path=/, no Domain), short Max-Age, server-side idle and absolute timeouts.
localStorage is readable by any script (XSS); memory is safer but lost on reload; neither is sent automatically.
Signed self-contained token. Easy to verify, hard to revoke, so keep it short lived; never store secrets inside, because the payload is only encoded.
Redirect to the authorization server, user signs in, code returns to the redirect URI, exchange code plus PKCE verifier for tokens. The implicit flow is obsolete.
A one-time random verifier and its hash (challenge) bind the code to the client that started the flow.
state protects the redirect from CSRF; nonce in OIDC binds the ID token to the session.
Long lived, so rotate on use or sender-constrain (DPoP), cap lifetime, and tie it to the user session so logout kills it.
Single-flight refresh in one place, handle 401 by refresh and retry once, and coordinate across tabs.
Server is the OAuth client, browser uses a cookie, server proxies API calls to an allow-list. Strongly recommended for sensitive data.
Backend does the code exchange and refresh, but hands the access token to the browser. Access token theft is still possible.
Everything in the SPA as a public client. Exposed to all attacks in the threat model; use only for low-risk apps.
SameSite, synchronizer token or signed double-submit, custom request header, Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site checks; no state changes on GET.
credentials: 'include' needs Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and a specific origin, not a wildcard. Preflight is triggered by custom headers.
Re-auth for sensitive actions, MFA or passkeys, rate limits, and WCAG 2.2 accessible authentication (no cognitive tests to log in).
Hides unfinished or risky code; short lived. Remove once at 100 percent.
Ramp 1, 10, 50, 100 percent with a stable hash per user, watching errors and Core Web Vitals between steps.
Splits users into variants to measure a metric; needs exposure events and enough sample size.
Kill switches and entitlement toggles can live longer. Entitlements must still be enforced on the server.

fe-feature-flags-client.s: Where and when the value is computed

k.d: User id, plan, country, device and app version sent with each evaluation; consistent bucketing needs a stable id (anonymous id before login).
Keep the same id across login or alias them so a user does not switch variants mid-session.
Server evaluates and inlines values so first paint is correct; the SDK then refreshes from the service.
Streaming for instant kill switches, polling for simplicity; cache last-known values for offline or outage.

fe-feature-flags-client.s: Keep flags from becoming a mess

k.d: Every flag read has a safe default if the service is unreachable. Prefer default off for new features.
Check a flag at one place per feature (a route, a component boundary), not scattered conditions; avoid nesting flags.
Owner, ticket and expiry date per flag; periodic report of stale flags; delete the dead branch and the flag together.
A vendor-neutral API: providers translate to the flag system, evaluation context carries user data, hooks add logging or telemetry.
Client SDK with React and Angular variants for browser apps.
Use an in-memory provider in tests to flip flags; cover both branches; run end-to-end with the new variant before ramp-up.
Tag errors and performance metrics with active flag variants so a bad rollout is easy to spot and roll back.
register(url, {scope}) ties the worker to an origin and path. It controls only pages inside its scope and needs HTTPS (localhost is allowed).
Runs once per new script. Use event.waitUntil() to precache the app shell; a failed addAll() fails the install.
A new version waits until old pages close. On activate, delete old caches.
Activates the new worker without waiting.
Lets the active worker take control of already-open pages.
The browser fetches the script on navigation, and on events if it has not checked in 24 hours. A byte difference starts a new install.

fe-service-worker.s: From the offline cookbook and Workbox

k.d: Answer from cache, fall back to the network. Best for versioned static assets and the usual choice for offline-first.
Try the network, use the cache if it fails. Good for fresh content, but slow networks wait before falling back, so add a timeout.
Serve the cached copy now and refresh it in the background for next time. Good for avatars and non-critical data.
Network only for analytics and non-GET requests. Cache only for files you precached at install.

fe-service-worker.s: What else a worker can do

k.d: A push event wakes the worker to show a notification, even with no tab open. Needs user permission.
A sync event runs when the network returns, ideal for sending a queued outbox. Limited browser availability.
No DOM, no localStorage, no synchronous APIs. It can be stopped when idle, so keep state in IndexedDB, not in variables.
The Cache API never expires entries. Version cache names and cap size and age, and handle QuotaExceededError.
A named collection of records, like a table but holding JavaScript objects. Any value the structured clone algorithm supports can be stored.
A keyPath reads the key from a property, autoIncrement generates one, or you pass it yourself on each add.
Let you look up records by another field, for example status or date. A unique index rejects duplicates and a compound index covers several fields.
openCursor with a key range walks results in order. getAll() reads a whole range at once.
Scoped to named stores, in readonly, readwrite or versionchange mode. Failing one aborts and rolls back all of it.
A transaction stays active only while requests are pending. Awaiting something that is not an IndexedDB request ends it, and the next request fails.
open(name, version) with an integer. onupgradeneeded is the only place to create or delete stores and indexes.
When a newer version is requested, other tabs get versionchange and should close their connection, otherwise the upgrade is blocked.
idb makes the API promise-based; Dexie adds a schema declaration, queries and liveQuery for reactive UI; localForage offers a simple key-value API.
Best-effort storage can be evicted under pressure. navigator.storage.estimate() reports usage; persist() requests protection. Safari may clear script-written data after 7 days without interaction.
Same-origin only, but an XSS bug can read it, so do not keep long-lived secrets there. Third-party iframes lose access when third-party cookies are blocked.
Offline data, drafts, outboxes, large caches and client-side search indexes; not for tiny flags, which can use Web Storage.
Key-value strings that persist after the browser closes, shared by every tab of the same origin. Serialize objects with JSON.
Like localStorage but separate per tab and cleared when the tab closes.
Synchronous, so it blocks the main thread; about 5 MiB; strings only; not available in workers. In private mode localStorage behaves like sessionStorage.
Fires in the other same-origin documents when storage changes, useful for cross-tab sync.

fe-web-storage-cookies.s: Small state the server and browser share

k.d: Three flags matter most.
JavaScript cannot read the cookie, limiting damage from XSS.
Sent only over HTTPS.
Strict: same-site only. Lax: also top-level navigations from elsewhere (the default). None: cross-site, and requires Secure.
Max-Age (seconds) takes precedence over Expires. Without either it is a session cookie. Delete by resending with Max-Age=0.
__Host- requires Secure, Path=/ and no Domain, so subdomains cannot overwrite the cookie. __Secure- requires Secure.
Set by embedded content and increasingly blocked by default, which can break widgets and cross-site sign-in.
Preference: localStorage. Draft for one tab: sessionStorage. Auth session: HttpOnly cookie. Big or structured data: IndexedDB. Network responses: Cache Storage.
One XSS bug can read and write all Web Storage on the origin, so never store session ids or secrets there (OWASP). Treat stored data as untrusted input.
Web Storage has no path scoping; every app on the origin shares it. Use separate subdomains for separate apps.
Wrap reads and writes in try/catch for QuotaExceededError and blocked storage, and let the app run without it.
Used by one script, created with new Worker(). The most common choice for off-main-thread compute.
Used by many tabs, iframes or workers of the same origin through message ports. It shuts down when nothing references it.
A special worker acting as a network proxy; see the Service Worker block. It is not for general computation.
Created with {type:'module'} so the worker can use import. Bundlers support new Worker(new URL(..., import.meta.url)).
postMessage copies data, including Dates and circular references, but not functions or DOM nodes.
ArrayBuffers and other transferables move with no copy, which matters for large data. The sender loses access.
Lets threads read and write the same memory without messaging, but brings concurrency and security concerns, so use it only with a clear need.
A tiny RPC layer built on postMessage and proxies: expose() in the worker, wrap() on the page, then call methods with await.
Parsing big JSON or CSV, client-side search, image and audio processing, syntax highlighting, encryption and WebAssembly libraries.
Keep the main thread for input and rendering. Tasks over 50 ms are long tasks that raise INP.
Starting a worker, copying data and extra code are overhead, so measure first. Workers cannot use the DOM, localStorage or most window APIs.
Call terminate() when finished, handle onerror, and set CSP headers on the worker script because workers do not inherit the page policy.

fe-browser-http-cache.s: Can the browser reuse it without asking?

k.d: The number of seconds a response stays fresh. After that it is stale and must be revalidated before reuse.
A shared cache reports elapsed time in Age. With no explicit lifetime, caches may guess, typically 10% of the time since Last-Modified, so always set Cache-Control.
Says the content will never change, so the browser need not revalidate even on reload.
After max-age, serve the stale copy immediately for a set window while fetching a fresh one in the background. Defined in RFC 5861.
The server tags a version; the client sends the tag back and gets 304 Not Modified if it still matches.
A date-based validator used with If-Modified-Since. If both are present, If-None-Match takes precedence; send both.
no-cache: store but always revalidate. no-store: never store. must-revalidate forbids serving stale after expiry.

fe-browser-http-cache.s: What to send for each kind of file

k.d: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The hash in the filename is the cache buster.
Cache-Control: no-cache (often with private) plus an ETag, so users get new asset links after each deploy.
private, plus short max-age or stale-while-revalidate where slightly old is fine; no-store for data that must never hit disk.
Makes the cache key depend on request headers such as Accept-Language. Avoid Vary: User-Agent and vary on Cookie; use private instead.

fe-bundler-code-splitting.s: From many source files to a few browser-ready files

k.d: The bundler starts at an entry file and follows every import to build a graph of all code the app needs. Everything else (minify, split, hash) works on this graph.
import and export are static, so a tool can read them without running the code. This is what makes tree shaking and safe splitting possible.
require() can be dynamic, so bundlers cannot prove what is unused. Prefer ES module builds of packages.
TypeScript, JSX and modern syntax are compiled for your target browsers, then minified. esbuild and Rolldown do this very quickly because they are written in Go and Rust.
Vite serves source files as native ES modules in development for instant start, and creates an optimised bundle only for production.
The bundler marks which exports are used and drops the rest. It relies on static import and export statements.
A module that does something on import (patches a global, registers a style) cannot be dropped. Packages declare sideEffects in package.json so unused modules can be removed safely.

Importing a whole library object (import _ from 'lodash') pulls everything; import the single function or use an ES build. Barrel files (index.ts re-exporting all) can defeat shaking if modules have side effects.

fe-bundler-code-splitting.s: Cut the output into chunks loaded when needed

k.d: Several entries make several bundles, but shared modules get duplicated. Fine for separate pages, weak for one app.
SplitChunksPlugin in webpack (and Rollup/Rolldown chunking in Vite) pulls code used by many chunks into common files. A vendor chunk keeps rarely changing libraries cacheable.
The recommended way. Each import() is a split point, returns a promise, and can be wrapped with React.lazy and Suspense.
One chunk per route. The biggest, simplest win.
Lazy-load heavy widgets (rich text editor, chart, map) when they are first shown.
webpackPrefetch fetches a chunk when idle for a future navigation; webpackPreload fetches it in parallel for the current one.

fe-bundler-code-splitting.s: Keep it fast after the first visit and stop it growing

k.d: File names include a hash of their content, so they can be cached as immutable and a change gets a fresh URL.
A treemap of what is inside each chunk (webpack-bundle-analyzer, rollup-plugin-visualizer) shows the big dependencies to replace or lazy-load.
Fail the build when JavaScript passes a limit, for example with Lighthouse CI or bundlesize. A common starting point is 170 KB of critical-path resources, compressed.
More nodes mean more memory and more work for style, layout and paint. Updates after an interaction get slower as the DOM grows, which hurts INP.
Lighthouse warns at 800 nodes and treats the DOM as excessive above 1,400.

k.t: Infinite loading alone is not enough
k.d: Appending pages keeps the first render small, but the DOM keeps growing as the user scrolls.

fe-virtualized-list.s: Render the window, fake the rest

k.d: From scrollTop and viewport height, work out the first and last visible index. Render only those rows.
A tall spacer (or total height) keeps the scrollbar honest; rows are placed with absolute position or translateY.
Render a few extra rows on each side so quick scrolling does not show blanks.
Fixed heights are simplest. Variable heights use an estimate, then measure each row once rendered and correct the offsets.
ResizeObserver reports real heights. Cache them so scrolling back does not re-measure.
The same idea works across columns and in two directions for spreadsheets and galleries.

fe-virtualized-list.s: Use the lightest tool that works

k.d: Simple, linkable and accessible. Often the right answer when users can reasonably filter or search.
Lets the browser skip rendering of off-screen sections. Set contain-intrinsic-size so the scrollbar is stable. Cut one demo from 232 ms to 30 ms.
Fetch more data near the end of the list; react-window-infinite-loader and TanStack Query both pair with virtualization.
Unrendered rows are invisible to Ctrl+F and screen readers. Use aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex and offer search.
Rows unmount when scrolled away, so keep input values and expanded state in the parent or store.
Save the measured scroll offset when leaving and restore it on return; an index alone is approximate with dynamic heights.
Watches a target against a root (the viewport by default) and calls you when it crosses thresholds. Asynchronous, so it avoids the layout work of scroll handlers.
A tiny empty element after the last item. When it becomes visible, fetch the next page.
Grows or shrinks the root box, for example '400px 0px' fires 400px early so the data is ready before the reader arrives.

fe-infinite-scroll.s: How the API hands out pages

k.d: page or offset number. Simple, but inserts and deletes shift later pages and large offsets are slow on big tables.
An opaque pointer to the last item seen (after=abc). Stable under inserts and fast. Clients treat it as a black box so the server can change how it works.
Relay's GraphQL pattern: edges with cursor and node, plus pageInfo with hasNextPage and endCursor.
Stores pages in one cache entry. getNextPageParam reads the cursor from the last page; fetchNextPage loads more; hasNextPage and isFetchingNextPage drive the UI.
When stale, pages refetch one by one from the first to avoid stale cursors. maxPages limits memory and refetch cost.
Merge by id so a shifted item does not appear twice.
A real button keeps keyboard users and the footer reachable.
Remember offset and cursor so Back returns to the same place.
Show skeleton rows while loading and an inline retry if a page fails, without losing the pages already shown.
Virtualize the combined list once it passes a few hundred rows.

fe-image-pipeline-responsive.s: Smaller files for the same picture

k.d: Modern formats that compress better than JPEG and PNG, supported by all modern browsers. Use a JPEG or PNG fallback.
SVG for logos and icons (vector, scales free); PNG when you need lossless with transparency; JPEG, WebP or AVIF for photos.
Test a few quality levels and compare file size against visible quality.
srcset lists files with their widths (w descriptors); sizes says how wide the slot is. The browser combines these with screen size and pixel ratio.
Use w with sizes for fluid layouts; use x (1x, 2x) for fixed-size images such as logos.
